Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/generative-ai/pretrained-models)

</details>

### D3-027

*Objective: Select the best model for a given task based on common metrics generated in experiments*

A Generative AI Engineer logged three LLM candidates as runs in an MLflow experiment, all
evaluated on the same dataset with the same judges. The requirement: p95 latency under
2 seconds and a safety pass rate of 100%, then maximise correctness.
Run X: correctness 0.93, safety 100%, p95 3.9 s.
Run Y: correctness 0.88, safety 97%, p95 1.2 s.
Run Z: correctness 0.85, safety 100%, p95 1.5 s.
Which run should be selected?

- **A.** Run X, because it has the highest correctness
- **B.** Run Y, because it has the best balance of correctness and latency
- **C.** None, because correctness must be at least 0.90
- **D.** Run Z, because it is the only run that meets both hard constraints

<details>
<summary>Answer: D</summary>

Apply the hard constraints first. Run X fails latency (3.9 s) and Run Y fails safety (97%).
Only Run Z satisfies both, so it is selected even though its correctness is the lowest. A
ignores the latency constraint. B ignores the safety constraint. C invents a threshold that
is not in the requirement.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/)

</details>

### D3-028 · *choose two*

*Objective: Select the best model for a given task based on common metrics generated in experiments*

A Generative AI Engineer will compare a 70B and an 8B model for a RAG assistant and wants the
comparison in MLflow to be fair and actionable. Which TWO practices should they follow?

- **A.** Evaluate each model on a different, freshly sampled question set to avoid overfitting
- **B.** Run both candidates with mlflow.genai.evaluate() on the same evaluation dataset and the same scorers, logging each as a run with its configuration
- **C.** Compare only the perplexity of each model on the source documents
- **D.** Record operational metrics such as latency and token usage alongside judge scores, then compare runs side by side in the MLflow UI
- **E.** Pick the model whose responses look better on the first three examples

<details>
<summary>Answer: B, D</summary>

A fair comparison holds the data and judges constant and changes only the model (B), so score
differences can be attributed to the model. Decisions also need cost and latency next to
quality (D), and MLflow traces capture latency and token usage. A is wrong because different
datasets confound the comparison. C is wrong because perplexity does not measure task
correctness or groundedness. E is anecdotal and not statistically meaningful.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/tracing/)

</details>

### D3-029

*Objective: Utilize MLflow and Agent Framework for developing agentic systems*

A Generative AI Engineer is authoring a new tool-calling agent in LangGraph that will be
deployed on Databricks. It should support streaming, return intermediate tool-call messages,
and work with AI Playground, evaluation, and monitoring. Which MLflow interface does Databricks
recommend for wrapping the agent?

- **A.** mlflow.pyfunc.ResponsesAgent
- **B.** mlflow.pyfunc.ChatModel
- **C.** mlflow.pyfunc.ChatAgent
- **D.** A plain mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel with a free-form dict output

<details>
<summary>Answer: A</summary>

Databricks recommends ResponsesAgent for building agents. It is compatible with the OpenAI
Responses schema, returns multiple messages including tool calls, streams, works with any
framework, and integrates with Playground, evaluation, and monitoring. B and C are legacy
interfaces that are still supported but not recommended for new agents; many older prep
materials name ChatAgent. D loses the standard schema and the integrations.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/generative-ai/agent-framework/author-agent) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/generative-ai/agent-framework/agent-legacy-schema)

</details>

### D3-030

*Objective: Utilize MLflow and Agent Framework for developing agentic systems*

A Generative AI Engineer's agent object holds an HTTP client and a vector search client.
Logging it with standard pickling fails with serialisation errors. The team also wants the
agent definition to be reviewable in git. Which MLflow approach should they use?

- **A.** Save the agent object with Python's pickle module to a UC volume and load it at serving time
- **B.** Convert the agent to ONNX before logging
- **C.** Define the agent in a Python file that calls mlflow.models.set_model(agent), and log that file (models from code)
- **D.** Log only the prompt template and rebuild the agent manually in production

<details>
<summary>Answer: C</summary>

With models from code, you write the agent in a Python script, mark the model object with
mlflow.models.set_model(), and log the script instead of a pickled object. This avoids
serialising clients and keeps the definition in readable source. A repeats the failing
approach. B does not apply to an orchestration agent with tool clients. D breaks
reproducibility and the link between the logged model and what is deployed.

Docs: [1](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/serving/responses-agent/)

</details>

### D3-031

*Objective: Utilize MLflow and Agent Framework for developing agentic systems*

A Generative AI Engineer's LangGraph agent sometimes returns wrong order statuses. They need
to see, for a specific failing request, which tools were called, with what arguments, what each
returned, and how long each step took. What should they do?

- **A.** Inspect the serving endpoint's CPU utilisation chart
- **B.** Enable MLflow Tracing (e.g. mlflow.langchain.autolog()) and inspect the trace's spans for that request
- **C.** Increase the agent's logging level to print the final answer
- **D.** Re-run the evaluation dataset and compare the average correctness score

<details>
<summary>Answer: B</summary>

MLflow Tracing records the inputs, outputs, latency, and token usage of every intermediate step
as spans, including LLM calls and tool calls. LangGraph is covered by LangChain autologging.
A is wrong because infrastructure metrics do not show agent decisions. C shows only the final
output, not intermediate tool calls. D gives an aggregate score, not the step-level detail of
the failing request.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/tracing/)

</details>

### D3-032

*Objective: Utilize MLflow and Agent Framework for developing agentic systems*

A Generative AI Engineer wants an agent to compute shipping surcharges using a business rule
that finance already maintains. The rule must be governed, reusable across agents, executable
only by authorised principals, and deterministic. Which approach fits best?

- **A.** Describe the surcharge rule in the system prompt and let the LLM compute it
- **B.** Store the rule as text in the vector index so the agent can retrieve it
- **C.** Hard-code the rule separately inside each agent's Python file
- **D.** Implement the rule as a Unity Catalog function and give it to the agent as a tool (e.g. via UCFunctionToolkit), with EXECUTE granted to authorised principals

<details>
<summary>Answer: D</summary>

Unity Catalog functions are governed objects. Access is controlled with EXECUTE privileges,
they are reusable across agents, and they run deterministic code. UCFunctionToolkit exposes
them as agent tools. A and B are wrong because they rely on the LLM to perform exact business
calculations, which is non-deterministic and error-prone. C is wrong because it duplicates
logic, loses central governance, and lets agents drift apart.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/generative-ai/agent-framework/create-custom-tool)

</details>

### D3-033

*Objective: Compare the evaluation and monitoring phases of the Gen AI application life cycle*

A Generative AI Engineer explains the GenAI lifecycle to a new team member. Which statement
correctly contrasts evaluation and monitoring in MLflow 3 on Databricks?

- **A.** Evaluation runs only in production, and monitoring runs only in development
- **B.** Monitoring requires a labelled ground-truth dataset for every production request
- **C.** Evaluation scores a curated dataset with mlflow.genai.evaluate() to compare versions before release, while monitoring runs the same kinds of scorers on a sample of live production traces
- **D.** Monitoring is unnecessary if the evaluation dataset passed before deployment

<details>
<summary>Answer: C</summary>

Databricks positions evaluation as running mlflow.genai.evaluate() on an evaluation dataset to
score and compare app versions. Monitoring runs the same scorers automatically on a sample of
production traffic. A reverses the phases. B is wrong because production traffic is usually
unlabelled, which is why monitoring relies on judges that need no ground truth. D is wrong
because real traffic, data, and dependencies drift after release.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/production-monitoring)

</details>

### D3-034 · *choose two*

*Objective: Compare the evaluation and monitoring phases of the Gen AI application life cycle*

A Generative AI Engineer is setting up production monitoring for a RAG agent. Production
requests have no reference answers. Which TWO built-in judges can run on sampled production
traces without ground truth?

- **A.** RetrievalGroundedness
- **B.** Correctness
- **C.** RetrievalSufficiency
- **D.** Exact-match accuracy against expected answers
- **E.** Safety

<details>
<summary>Answer: A, E</summary>

RetrievalGroundedness checks whether the response is supported by the retrieved context, and
Safety checks for harmful content. Neither needs expectations, so both suit unlabelled live
traces. B (Correctness) and C (RetrievalSufficiency) require expected facts or answers, which
production traffic lacks. D needs a reference answer by definition. Ground-truth judges belong
to the evaluation phase, where curated expectations exist.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/concepts/judges/) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/production-monitoring)

</details>

### D3-035

*Objective: Enable multi-agent systems to leverage Genie Spaces or conversational API to retrieve data*

A Generative AI Engineer is building an assistant that must answer questions such as "How did
returns by region change month over month this year?" from sales tables in Unity Catalog. It
must also answer "What does the returns policy say about damaged goods?" from policy PDFs.
Users ask many novel analytical questions. Which architecture fits best?

- **A.** A supervisor agent that routes analytical questions to a Genie Space agent over the sales tables and policy questions to a Vector Search RAG agent
- **B.** Embed every sales table row into the vector index and use one RAG agent for everything
- **C.** Write a separate Unity Catalog SQL function for each anticipated analytical question
- **D.** Fine-tune the LLM on the sales tables so it can answer analytics directly

<details>
<summary>Answer: A</summary>

Structured aggregate questions are a natural-language-to-SQL problem, which Genie handles
over curated tables. Policy text is a retrieval problem. A supervisor coordinates the two
specialists. B is wrong because vector similarity cannot compute aggregates such as
month-over-month changes. C is wrong because fixed functions only cover anticipated questions,
while Genie can write new queries. D is wrong because the model would memorise stale numbers
and could not compute fresh aggregations.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/generative-ai/agent-framework/multi-agent-genie) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/generative-ai/agent-bricks/multi-agent-supervisor)

</details>

### D3-036

*Objective: Enable multi-agent systems to leverage Genie Spaces or conversational API to retrieve data*

A Generative AI Engineer is writing a custom tool that lets an agent query a Genie Space
through the Genie Conversation API. Which sequence correctly retrieves the tabular answer to a
new question?

- **A.** Call the Genie space's SQL warehouse directly with the natural-language question as the SQL text
- **B.** POST to start-conversation for the space, poll the returned message until its status is complete, then GET the attachment's query-result
- **C.** Upload the question to a UC volume and wait for Genie to write results to a Delta table
- **D.** Call the start-conversation endpoint once and read the table rows from its immediate HTTP response body

<details>
<summary>Answer: B</summary>

The Conversation API is asynchronous. Start a conversation with POST
/api/2.0/genie/spaces/{space_id}/start-conversation, poll the message (Databricks suggests
every 1-5 seconds with backoff) until it completes, then fetch the SQL attachment's
query-result. Follow-up questions use the conversation's messages endpoint. A is wrong because a
warehouse executes SQL, not natural language. C is not how Genie works. D is wrong because the
initial response returns identifiers and status, not finished results.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/api/genie/v1/conversation) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/genie/conversation-api)

</details>


<a id="domain-4"></a>

## Domain 4 — Assembling and Deploying Applications (22%)


<a id="domain-5"></a>

## Domain 5 — Governance (8%)

### D5-001

*Objective: Use masking techniques as guard rails to meet a performance objective*

A Generative AI Engineer runs an internal IT helpdesk assistant that must keep at least 96%
of sessions answered without a human handoff. Logs show that 7% of user messages include an
employee's personal phone number or email address, which security says must never reach the
LLM provider or the logs. The answers never depend on those values.
Which approach meets both the security requirement and the success target?

- **A.** Block every request in which PII is detected and return a default message
- **B.** Detect PII at the endpoint and mask it with placeholders before the request reaches the model, also masking PII in responses
- **C.** Add a system prompt instruction telling the model never to repeat phone numbers or email addresses
- **D.** Lower the temperature so the model is less likely to reproduce personal details

<details>
<summary>Answer: B</summary>

Masking replaces each PII span with a placeholder such as [EMAIL], so the value never reaches
the model or the logs while the request still gets answered; since answers do not need the
values, the success rate is preserved. A is wrong because blocking 7% of sessions caps the
answered rate near 93%, below the 96% target. C is wrong because the model still receives the
PII, so it reaches the provider and the logs; a prompt rule is not masking. D is wrong because
temperature does not remove data from the input and gives no privacy guarantee.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/configure-ai-gateway-endpoints) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/overview-serving-endpoints)

</details>

### D5-002 · *choose two*

*Objective: Use masking techniques as guard rails to meet a performance objective*

A Generative AI Engineer is building a RAG index over a Unity Catalog table of support
tickets. The table has a customer_email column and a free-text body that sometimes contains
phone numbers. Retrieval latency must not increase, and only the support-admins group may
ever see raw emails when querying the table.
Which TWO actions should the engineer take?

- **A.** Apply a Unity Catalog column mask on customer_email that returns the raw value only for members of the support-admins group
- **B.** Keep the raw data in the index and add a post-retrieval regex step on every request to strip emails and phone numbers
- **C.** Grant SELECT on the table to all users and rely on a disclaimer in the assistant's answers
- **D.** Redact phone numbers in the body text in the ingestion pipeline, for example with an AI function such as ai_mask, before chunking and embedding
- **E.** Move the tickets to a CSV file in a volume so Unity Catalog permissions no longer apply

<details>
<summary>Answer: A, D</summary>

A column mask is a SQL UDF that returns the original or masked value depending on the caller,
which meets the "only support-admins see raw emails" rule without duplicating tables (A).
Redacting PII in the free text before embedding is done once, offline, so it adds no
per-request latency and keeps PII out of the index (D). B adds work to every request, which
risks the latency objective, and the raw PII still sits in the index. C exposes PII to
everyone; a disclaimer is not a control. E removes governance instead of adding it.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/row-and-column-filters) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/mlflow3/genai/tracing/redact-pii-otel-traces)

</details>

### D5-003

*Objective: Use masking techniques as guard rails to meet a performance objective*

A Generative AI Engineer enabled MLflow tracing on a customer-service agent. Auditors find
that the stored traces contain customers' card numbers that users typed into the chat. The
agent's answer quality and latency must not change, but the traces must not keep the card
numbers.
What should the engineer do?

- **A.** Disable tracing for the agent entirely
- **B.** Block all chat messages that contain digits
- **C.** Register a span processor that redacts card numbers from span inputs and outputs before traces are exported
- **D.** Ask the LLM to remove card numbers from its own final answer

<details>
<summary>Answer: C</summary>

MLflow span processors run in the agent process and edit span inputs and outputs before the
trace is exported, so the stored trace never holds the raw value while the agent's behaviour
is unchanged. A removes the observability needed for evaluation and monitoring. B blocks many
legitimate messages (order numbers, dates) and hurts the success rate. D only affects the
final answer; the card number would still be stored in the input spans of the trace.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/mlflow3/genai/tracing/redact-pii-otel-traces)

</details>

### D5-004

*Objective: Select guardrail techniques to protect against malicious user inputs to a Gen AI application*

A Generative AI Engineer is deploying a procurement agent that can read purchase orders and
call a tool that approves payments. A red-team test shows that a user can phrase a request
so the agent calls the approval tool for an invoice the user does not own.
Which change most directly reduces the impact of this attack?

- **A.** Switch to a larger LLM that follows the system prompt more reliably
- **B.** Add a sentence to the system prompt stating that the agent must never approve unauthorized invoices
- **C.** Increase the number of retrieved purchase orders so the agent has more context
- **D.** Run the tool with least-privilege credentials scoped to the calling user and require explicit human confirmation before any payment approval

<details>
<summary>Answer: D</summary>

The risk is a harmful action, so the control must sit outside the model: if the tool only
runs with the caller's own permissions and a human must confirm approvals, a successful prompt
attack still cannot approve someone else's invoice. A and B depend on the model obeying,
which is exactly what prompt injection defeats; the attacker uses the same text channel as the
system prompt. C changes retrieval breadth and does nothing to restrict actions.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/generative-ai/agent-framework/deploy-agent) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/ai-governance)

</details>

### D5-005 · *choose two*

*Objective: Select guardrail techniques to protect against malicious user inputs to a Gen AI application*

A Generative AI Engineer serves a public-facing chatbot through a pay-per-token Foundation
Model API endpoint. Users are submitting jailbreak prompts to obtain harmful content, and some
users send thousands of requests per minute to brute-force the jailbreaks.
Which TWO controls should the engineer configure?

- **A.** Raise the endpoint's max_tokens so refusals are explained in more detail
- **B.** Enable the safety guardrail on the endpoint to filter unsafe content in requests and responses
- **C.** Turn on scale to zero for the endpoint
- **D.** Add few-shot examples of polite answers to the prompt
- **E.** Configure per-user rate limits on the endpoint

<details>
<summary>Answer: B, E</summary>

The safety guardrail (Databricks documents Llama Guard as the legacy safety filter) blocks
unsafe requests and responses and returns a default message, addressing harmful content (B).
Per-user rate limits cap how fast any single user can retry attacks and protect cost (E).
A increases output size and cost without stopping anything. C is a cost setting for idle
endpoints, not a security control. D shapes style but does not stop a determined jailbreak.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/configure-ai-gateway-endpoints) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/overview-serving-endpoints)

</details>

### D5-006

*Objective: Select guardrail techniques to protect against malicious user inputs to a Gen AI application*

A Generative AI Engineer deployed an agent with Agent Framework. The agent calls a
Foundation Model API endpoint for generation. The security team wants AI Gateway safety
filtering applied, but the engineer finds the legacy AI Guardrails settings are not supported
on the agent's own serving endpoint.
What is the best way to apply the safety filter?

- **A.** Enable the safety guardrail on the Foundation Model API endpoint that the agent calls, and keep checks in agent code where needed
- **B.** Redeploy the agent as a custom model endpoint, which supports AI Guardrails
- **C.** Skip safety filtering, because agents are protected automatically by Unity Catalog
- **D.** Add the word "safe" to every user prompt before it reaches the agent

<details>
<summary>Answer: A</summary>

In the legacy AI Gateway feature matrix, AI Guardrails are supported on external model,
pay-per-token and provisioned throughput endpoints but not on Databricks agent or custom model
endpoints, so the filter belongs on the LLM endpoint the agent calls, with extra checks in the
agent code if required. B is wrong because custom model endpoints do not support guardrails
either. C is wrong because Unity Catalog governs data access, not content safety. D is not a
control at all.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/overview-serving-endpoints)

</details>

### D5-007

*Objective: Use legal/licensing requirements for data sources to avoid legal risk*

A Generative AI Engineer at a software company wants to improve a paid product's
documentation assistant by adding a public Q&A dataset to the RAG index. The dataset's card
says it is released under CC BY-NC 4.0.
What should the engineer do?

- **A.** Use the dataset, since it is publicly downloadable
- **B.** Use the dataset but add a disclaimer to every answer that cites it
- **C.** Exclude the dataset and find a source whose license permits commercial use, or license the content
- **D.** Use the dataset only for embeddings, because embeddings are not covered by copyright

<details>
<summary>Answer: C</summary>

A non-commercial (NC) license forbids use in a commercial product, so the dataset cannot feed
a paid assistant; the fix is a commercially licensed or owned source. A confuses public
availability with permission. B is wrong because a disclaimer does not cure a license
violation. D is wrong because embedding and retrieving the text is still using the licensed
content, and the retrieved chunks are shown in the prompt and answers.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/machine-learning/foundation-model-apis/supported-models)

</details>

### D5-008

*Objective: Use legal/licensing requirements for data sources to avoid legal risk*

A Generative AI Engineer must prove to the legal team that a production RAG index was built
only from three approved, licensed Unity Catalog tables, and must keep that proof current as
pipelines change.
Which Databricks capability best supports this?

- **A.** The Vector Search query logs
- **B.** Unity Catalog lineage from the source tables to the table that feeds the index, with license tags on each source
- **C.** A Python comment at the top of the chunking notebook listing the sources
- **D.** The model card of the embedding model

<details>
<summary>Answer: B</summary>

Unity Catalog lineage records which tables feed downstream tables, so it shows automatically
and continuously what data produced the index source table; tags record each source's license.
A shows what was queried, not where the indexed data came from. C is manual and goes stale as
pipelines change. D describes the embedding model's license, not the provenance of the data.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/ai-governance) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/row-and-column-filters)

</details>

### D5-009

*Objective: Recommend an alternative for problematic text mitigation in a data source feeding a GenAI application*

A Generative AI Engineer finds that a shopping assistant sometimes quotes insulting language
from customer reviews that are indexed for RAG. About 2% of the 3 million reviews contain such
language. The index is a Delta Sync index on a Delta table.
What is the most effective fix?

- **A.** Add an instruction to the prompt asking the model not to repeat offensive words
- **B.** Lower the number of retrieved chunks from 10 to 3
- **C.** Fine-tune the LLM to ignore offensive context
- **D.** Score reviews with a toxicity classifier in the ingestion pipeline, remove or redact the flagged ones in the source table, and let the index sync

<details>
<summary>Answer: D</summary>

The problem is in the data, so fix it once upstream: cleaning the source table removes the
offending text from the Delta Sync index for every future request, and scanning new reviews
keeps it clean. A relies on the model's compliance on every request and fails silently. B only
makes toxic chunks less likely to appear and also removes useful context. C is expensive and
still leaves the toxic text in the prompt.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/configure-ai-gateway-endpoints)

</details>

### D5-010

*Objective: Recommend an alternative for problematic text mitigation in a data source feeding a GenAI application*

A Generative AI Engineer built an HR policy assistant on top of an employee discussion forum.
Reviewers find that many forum posts contain outdated policies, personal opinions, and biased
statements, and the assistant repeats them. The HR department maintains an official, reviewed
policy handbook.
What should the engineer recommend?

- **A.** Replace the forum with the official policy handbook as the primary source, keeping forum content out of the index unless it is reviewed
- **B.** Keep the forum and add an output safety filter
- **C.** Increase the chunk size so each forum post has more context
- **D.** Add the forum post's date to each chunk and ask the model to prefer recent posts

<details>
<summary>Answer: A</summary>

When most of a source is untrusted or low quality, the strongest mitigation is to replace it
with a curated, authoritative source; the handbook is reviewed and owned by HR. B catches
toxic content at best but not outdated or opinionated policy text. C does not change what the
text says. D still feeds opinions into the prompt and relies on the model to judge them, and a
recent post can still be wrong.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/ai-governance)

</details>


<a id="domain-6"></a>

## Domain 6 — Evaluation and Monitoring (12%)

### D6-001

*Objective: Select an LLM choice (size and architecture) based on a set of quantitative evaluation metrics*

A Generative AI Engineer compares four models on the same 400-question evaluation set for a
RAG assistant. Requirements: p95 latency at most 1.5 s, and the highest possible correctness
within that limit.
Model W: correctness 91%, p95 2.8 s.
Model X: correctness 76%, p95 0.7 s.
Model Y: correctness 87%, p95 1.3 s.
Model Z: correctness 84%, p95 1.1 s.
Which model should the engineer choose?

- **A.** Model W
- **B.** Model X
- **C.** Model Y
- **D.** Model Z

<details>
<summary>Answer: C</summary>

Apply the hard constraint first: W fails the 1.5 s latency limit, so it is out despite the
best correctness. Among X, Y and Z, Y has the highest correctness (87%) within the limit. X is
fastest but its quality is far lower, and the requirement asks for the best quality inside the
limit, not the lowest latency. Z also meets latency but scores below Y.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/evaluate-app)

</details>

### D6-002

*Objective: Select an LLM choice (size and architecture) based on a set of quantitative evaluation metrics*

A Generative AI Engineer must choose a model for a high-volume classification-and-explanation
task. Cost per 1,000 requests is the main constraint, and quality must be at least 85% on the
team's evaluation set.
Dense 70B: quality 90%, $4.10 per 1,000 requests.
Mixture-of-experts with a small active parameter count: quality 88%, $1.70.
Dense 8B: quality 79%, $0.35.
Dense 8B fine-tuned on the task: quality 86%, $0.55.
Which model should the engineer pick?

- **A.** Dense 8B fine-tuned on the task
- **B.** Mixture-of-experts model
- **C.** Dense 70B
- **D.** Dense 8B

<details>
<summary>Answer: A</summary>

With cost as the main constraint and an 85% quality floor, choose the cheapest model that
clears the floor: the fine-tuned 8B at 86% and $0.55. D is cheaper but fails the 85% floor.
B and C pass the floor but cost about 3x and 7x more; their extra quality is not what the
requirement prioritises. This shows how a small task-specific model can beat larger
architectures on the cost-quality frontier.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/evaluate-app)

</details>

### D6-003 · *choose two*

*Objective: Select key metrics to monitor for a specific LLM deployment scenario*

A Generative AI Engineer is launching a customer-facing streaming chat assistant that answers
product questions from retrieved documentation. Product managers worry about slow responses
and hallucinated answers.
Which TWO metrics are most important to monitor?

- **A.** p95 time to first token
- **B.** BLEU score against reference answers for each live request
- **C.** Groundedness of responses in the retrieved context, measured on sampled traces
- **D.** Average GPU temperature of the serving cluster
- **E.** Total number of documents in the source volume

<details>
<summary>Answer: A, C</summary>

In streaming chat, users perceive the time until the first token, and the tail (p95) captures
the slow experiences that the mean hides (A). Groundedness on sampled traces measures
hallucination without needing reference answers (C). B needs a reference answer for every live
request, which production traffic does not have. D is an infrastructure detail that does not
track either concern. E describes the corpus size, not answer speed or quality.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/production-monitoring) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/concepts/judges/)

</details>

### D6-004

*Objective: Select key metrics to monitor for a specific LLM deployment scenario*

A Generative AI Engineer runs a nightly job that uses ai_query() to summarise 4 million
support transcripts into a Delta table read by analysts the next morning.
Which metrics should the engineer prioritise for monitoring this deployment?

- **A.** p99 per-request latency and time to first token
- **B.** Job completion time, failed rows, total tokens processed, and cost per run
- **C.** Thumbs-up rate from end users
- **D.** Number of concurrent chat sessions

<details>
<summary>Answer: B</summary>

For a batch workload, no user waits on any single request; what matters is finishing before
the morning, how many rows failed, and how many tokens (and dollars) each run consumes. A
applies to interactive serving. C does not exist for a batch job with no chat interface. D is a
real-time chat metric unrelated to a nightly batch.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/admin/system-tables/model-serving-cost)

</details>

### D6-005

*Objective: Evaluate agent performance using MLflow scoring and tracing*

A Generative AI Engineer wants to evaluate a new version of a tool-calling agent on an
evaluation dataset using MLflow 3, with built-in LLM judges and one custom scorer, and keep a
trace for every evaluated row.
Which call should the engineer use?

- **A.** mlflow.evaluate(model=agent_uri, model_type="databricks-agent")
- **B.** mlflow.log_metric("quality", score)
- **C.** mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(agent_uri).predict(eval_df)
- **D.** mlflow.genai.evaluate(data=eval_dataset, predict_fn=agent_fn, scorers=[...])

<details>
<summary>Answer: D</summary>

In MLflow 3, mlflow.genai.evaluate() calls predict_fn for each row (producing a trace), runs the
listed scorers (built-in judges and custom scorers), and logs per-row assessments to an MLflow
run. A is the legacy Agent Evaluation API used by older material. B only logs a number you
already computed. C produces predictions but no scorers or evaluation results.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/evaluate-app)

</details>

### D6-006

*Objective: Evaluate agent performance using MLflow scoring and tracing*

A Generative AI Engineer's RAG agent scores poorly on the Correctness judge, but
RetrievalGroundedness is high on the same rows. The engineer opens the MLflow traces of failing
rows.
What is the most likely diagnosis to confirm in the traces?

- **A.** The LLM is inventing facts not present in the retrieved context
- **B.** The retriever span is returning documents that are irrelevant or outdated, and the LLM faithfully summarises them
- **C.** The evaluation dataset is missing the inputs field
- **D.** The Safety judge is overriding the Correctness judge

<details>
<summary>Answer: B</summary>

High groundedness means the answer is supported by the retrieved context; low correctness
means the answer disagrees with the expected facts. Together they point to retrieval: the
context itself is wrong, which the retriever span in the trace will show (low
RetrievalRelevance would confirm it). A would lower groundedness, not keep it high. C would
prevent evaluation from running at all. D is wrong because judges are independent and do not
override each other.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/concepts/judges/) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/tracing/)

</details>

### D6-007 · *choose two*

*Objective: Identify evaluation judges that require ground truth*

A Generative AI Engineer is building an evaluation dataset for a RAG application and wants to
know which built-in MLflow judges will need SMEs to supply expected facts for each row.
Which TWO judges require ground truth?

- **A.** RetrievalGroundedness
- **B.** Correctness
- **C.** RelevanceToQuery
- **D.** RetrievalSufficiency
- **E.** Safety

<details>
<summary>Answer: B, D</summary>

Correctness compares the response to expected facts or an expected response, and
RetrievalSufficiency checks whether the retrieved context contains what is needed to produce
the expected facts; both need expectations (B, D). RetrievalGroundedness compares the response
with the retrieved context, not a reference answer (A). RelevanceToQuery compares the response
with the request (C). Safety judges the response content on its own (E).

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/concepts/judges/) · [2](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/eval-monitor/scorers/llm-judge/predefined/)

</details>

### D6-008

*Objective: Identify evaluation judges that require ground truth*

A Generative AI Engineer wants to score live production traces of a deployed agent. No one
has written expected answers for these requests.
Which built-in judge is NOT suitable for this traffic without additional labeling?

- **A.** Correctness
- **B.** Guidelines
- **C.** RelevanceToQuery
- **D.** Safety

<details>
<summary>Answer: A</summary>

Correctness needs ground truth in the expectations field, which unlabeled production traffic
does not have; it becomes usable only after SMEs add expectations. Guidelines checks the
response against natural-language rules you define once, RelevanceToQuery compares the
response with the request, and Safety checks for harmful content; none of them needs an answer
key, so all three can run on live traces.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/concepts/judges/)

</details>

### D6-009

*Objective: Use Databricks custom Scorers for evaluating agents and LLMs*

A Generative AI Engineer's agent must return JSON containing the keys "category" and
"priority". The engineer wants every evaluation run to report the share of responses that meet
this rule, cheaply and deterministically.
What should the engineer do?

- **A.** Use the built-in Correctness judge with the schema in expected_facts
- **B.** Ask SMEs to check the format of each response in the Review App
- **C.** Write a Python function decorated with @scorer that parses outputs and returns True or False, and pass it in scorers to mlflow.genai.evaluate()
- **D.** Create an LLM judge that asks a model whether the output looks like JSON

<details>
<summary>Answer: C</summary>

A format rule is deterministic, so a code-based scorer is free, fast and exact: the @scorer
function receives outputs and can return a boolean or a Feedback, and it runs inside
mlflow.genai.evaluate(). A uses an LLM to judge factual correctness, which is the wrong tool for
a schema check. B spends scarce expert time on something code can verify. D is slower, costs
tokens and can be wrong on a question a JSON parser answers exactly.

Docs: [1](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/eval-monitor/scorers/custom/) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/custom-scorers)

</details>

### D6-010

*Objective: Use Databricks custom Scorers for evaluating agents and LLMs*

A Generative AI Engineer needs to grade an insurance agent's replies against a company rubric
with three outcomes: "compliant", "partially_compliant" and "non_compliant". The judgement
requires reading the request and the reply, and no built-in judge expresses this rubric.
Which approach fits best?

- **A.** A regular-expression scorer that searches for the word "compliant"
- **B.** The built-in RetrievalSufficiency judge
- **C.** Averaging the Safety and RelevanceToQuery scores
- **D.** A custom LLM judge created with make_judge(), with instructions that reference the inputs and outputs and a feedback value type limited to the three outcomes

<details>
<summary>Answer: D</summary>

make_judge() creates a custom LLM judge from natural-language instructions that use template
variables such as inputs and outputs, and feedback_value_type can restrict results to the
three categories. A cannot capture a judgement about meaning. B checks whether retrieved
context covers expected facts, which is not this rubric. C combines unrelated metrics and
cannot produce the three rubric outcomes.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/custom-judge/)

</details>

### D6-011

*Objective: Use inference logging to assess deployed RAG application performance*

A Generative AI Engineer routes 20% of a RAG endpoint's traffic to a new model version. A week
later, user complaints rise. Inference tables are enabled on the endpoint.
What is the best first analysis?

- **A.** Query the inference table grouped by the served entity to compare error rate and latency per version, then score sampled requests from each version for groundedness
- **B.** Delete the inference table and re-enable it to collect fresh data
- **C.** Re-run the offline evaluation dataset only on the old version
- **D.** Increase the endpoint's provisioned concurrency

<details>
<summary>Answer: A</summary>

The inference table records each request and response with the served entity, status and
timing, so grouping by version isolates whether the new version causes the regression; scoring
sampled requests per version adds the quality dimension. B throws away the evidence. C ignores
the new version and real traffic. D assumes a capacity problem without any data.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/inference-tables-serving-endpoints)

</details>

### D6-012

*Objective: Use inference tables and Agent Monitoring to track a live LLM endpoint*

A Generative AI Engineer wants continuous quality tracking of a deployed agent that handles
100,000 requests per day, using the same Safety judge already used in offline evaluation,
while keeping judge costs low.
What should the engineer do?

- **A.** Run mlflow.genai.evaluate() manually every morning on all of yesterday's requests with Correctness and Safety
- **B.** Register the Safety scorer to the agent's MLflow experiment and start it with a sampling configuration that evaluates a fraction of traces
- **C.** Read the inference table weekly and grep responses for unsafe words
- **D.** Ask users to report unsafe answers by email

<details>
<summary>Answer: B</summary>

Production monitoring runs registered scorers on traces automatically; calling start() with a
sampling rate judges a fraction of traffic, reusing the offline scorer and controlling LLM-judge
cost. A is manual, judges every request (expensive), and Correctness cannot run without ground
truth. C is slow and keyword matching misses most unsafe content. D is not monitoring and
captures only a small, biased share of problems.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/production-monitoring)

</details>

### D6-013 · *choose two*

*Objective: Use AI Gateway (Inference Tables, Usage Tables, and rate limiting) to track an LLM or agent deployed via Agent Framework.*

A Generative AI Engineer deployed an agent with Agent Framework that calls a pay-per-token
Foundation Model API endpoint. Finance wants to know how many tokens each team's service
principal consumes, and wants to stop one team from consuming more than its share.
Which TWO actions should the engineer take?

- **A.** Read token counts from the agent endpoint's inference table request column
- **B.** Enable scale to zero on the Foundation Model API endpoint
- **C.** Enable usage tracking on the Foundation Model API endpoint and query the usage system table grouped by requester
- **D.** Add a Guidelines judge that tells the agent to use fewer tokens
- **E.** Configure a token-per-minute rate limit for that team's service principal on the Foundation Model API endpoint

<details>
<summary>Answer: C, E</summary>

Usage tracking writes per-request token counts and the requester to system tables, which is
the right source for consumption by principal (C). A rate limit for a specific service
principal caps that team's usage, and TPM limits belong on the LLM endpoint because agent
endpoints support only QPM limits (E). A is wrong because inference tables record payloads,
and token accounting by requester is the purpose of usage tables. B affects idle capacity, not
one team's consumption. D is an evaluation tool, not an enforcement mechanism.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/configure-ai-gateway-endpoints) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/overview-serving-endpoints) · [3](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/usage-tracking)

</details>

### D6-014

*Objective: Use Databricks features to control LLM costs*

A Generative AI Engineer's development team has an LLM endpoint on provisioned throughput that
is used for about one hour a day for testing. The monthly bill is high, and the team accepts
slower first responses.
Which change most reduces cost?

- **A.** Add more provisioned throughput units to finish tests faster
- **B.** Enable inference tables on the endpoint
- **C.** Use pay-per-token Foundation Model APIs or enable scale to zero for the endpoint
- **D.** Switch to a larger model so fewer tests are needed

<details>
<summary>Answer: C</summary>

Provisioned throughput charges for reserved capacity whether or not it is used, so an endpoint
idle 23 hours a day wastes most of its cost; pay-per-token charges only for tokens, and scale
to zero removes idle capacity at the price of a cold start, which the team accepts. A adds more
reserved capacity and raises cost. B adds logging, which costs more, not less. D raises
per-token cost.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/admin/system-tables/model-serving-cost) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/machine-learning/foundation-model-apis/supported-models)

</details>

### D6-015

*Objective: Incorporate SME feedback to improve agent performance*

A Generative AI Engineer uses a custom LLM judge to score a claims-processing agent. SMEs have
labeled 120 traces in a labeling session using a calibrated rubric, and the judge agrees with
them on only 64% of traces. The engineer wants automated evaluation that reflects the SMEs'
standard.
What should the engineer do?

- **A.** Stop using SME labels and trust the judge, since it is more consistent
- **B.** Remove the traces where the judge and SMEs disagree from the evaluation dataset
- **C.** Replace the judge with the built-in Safety judge
- **D.** Align the judge with the SME feedback on those traces, verify agreement improves, and then use the aligned judge in mlflow.genai.evaluate()

<details>
<summary>Answer: D</summary>

MLflow supports aligning an LLM judge with human assessments: the judge's align() method uses
traces that carry both judge and SME feedback to produce a judge that better matches the
experts, which can then be used as a scorer. A treats a disagreeing judge as truth over
calibrated experts. B hides the cases that most need attention and inflates agreement. C
measures harmful content, not the claims-processing rubric.

Docs: [1](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/eval-monitor/align-judges) · [2](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/mlflow3/genai/human-feedback/expert-feedback/label-existing-traces)

</details>
